title: Penny in the Dust, Text C
text:
This is the novel Penny in the Dust written by Ernest Buckler. The characters are Father, Mother, sister, and Dan. The novel is about Dan’s memories of Father and the penny and it tells about Father’s love. This extract comes from the rising action of Penny in the dust. It is a flashback of Dan’s childhood about the penny. In this extract, we can get insight into Dan's emotions and we can see his trust in his father.
This extract uses 2 ways to convey Dan’s feelings to readers dramatically.
The first one is the repetition of the expression ‘How could I ~?’. It emphasizes Dan’s emotions and lets readers empathize with his feelings. It is shown in these phrases, like “How could I bear the shame of repeating”, “How could I explain that pit-of-the-stomach sickness” and “How could I explain that I wasn’t really hiding from them?” These sentences are interrogative sentences, but they do not intend to question. These are the expressions to show Dan’s feelings. The happening that lost the penny is just a trivial matter to us or other characters but, it was a serious matter to Dan. The expressions make readers empathize with Dan’s emotions. And also, it makes emotion maximized through repetition. It makes an emotional impact on the extract.
Next is the point of view. It is a first-person perspective. We can see it through phrases such as “I never dreamed of father ever mentioning it again.” The first-person point of view allows readers to observe Dan’s emotions and Dan’s trust in his father. It makes readers can understand him and assimilate him. It gives the reader empathy and understanding of Dan's experiences. “I might have known he would find it.” Especially this sentence shows Dan’s trust in his father. It conveys Dan's belief in his father with his trust and love for his father.
Follow-up Questions (4~5min)
15. What is symbolic in this story? Explain its symbolism.
The ‘penny’ is the symbol of this story. It symbolizes the love of the son and father. It was shown that the penny is a valuable thing for Dan. At the end of the story, it also becomes important to his father because the penny shows the son’s love for his father. Dan was so depressed when he lost his penny and he wanted to find it. Because he had the penny with the desire to spend more time with his father. It was the love for his father. after that, his father noticed his thoughts and emotion.
So it became a symbol of the son and father’s love and relationship. Actually, a penny is a worthless thing generally. However, it revealed the meaning of the penny for Dan, and it got worth it.
16. Describe the father in this story in as much detail as you can. What can we tell about him by his actions?
The father was shown to Dan he was a capable father. The father lacked emotional expression, but he was careful to enter the world of his son Dan because he knew his son was very creative and his own world was vast. He respected Dan’s world. The father didn’t express his emotion well, but he always helped his son to solve some problems, for example, he fixed the handle of the wheelbarrow and untangled fishing line. In addition, he was running through the burning brush to find his son and trying to find the penny for his son. His action like this shows his love for his son. So Dan trusted his father and Dan thought his father would find him soon when he was in his bed. The father didn’t express his love directly, but his love appeared through his action indirectly.
General Discussion (5~6min)
Social organization: Love in the Family How does the love in the family affect people growing up?
Do you think “communication” is the most effective way to socialize with others? Of course, I think so. I think communication is important to get along with others or solve some problems in our community and relationships. We always meet many people, have conversations with others, and work together in our life. We don’t live alone. We have to live together. When we have a lot of time with people, sometimes we get in trouble. Then communication is essential and a great way to solve the problem. We can get along with others through communication.

title: Theater Review: <Who>
text:
This theater <Who> is created by English theater class students. It is about the implicit bias and discrimination we might have.
In this story, a man was murdered in a village, and the next day, the village foreman let gathering village people. There are five people in a room that is locked. They had never met, and there is one person who is a criminal. They notice they can’t get out of there, so they are embarrassed. One is the teacher, the other one is a single mother, the other one is a village foreman, the other one is a foreigner, and the other one is a gangster. They believe the culprit is in there tacitly. So they start to guess the culprit. However, they lose their composure and show their bias while they guess. Then, who is the culprit?
<Who> shows the naked appearance of our bias and discrimination effectively. Their bias is shown in their words and attitude. It lets us think back on our thought and judgment. It can seem just a mystery drama, but it isn’t. This play is a social criticism under the guise of a mystery play. It reveals the biases we might have. This play has the ability to make the audience think. After watching this play, I found myself thinking about what the story is about and what the message aims to convey.
There were only a table and chairs on the stage, and the actors sat down on the chairs. Their movement remained in the middle of the stage, so it was limited. Thanks to the limited movement, it was possible to more focus on the characters and lines. In addition, the relationship and attitudes between the characters were clearly visible. The bias mixed in words could be seen more clearly by focusing on lines rather than actions. Also, the pin light used in the monologue allowed me to focus on the character, and the red light made the murder scene look more creepy.
I think this play is incredibly meaningful and thought-provoking. <Who> is a fantastic play. I believe you must see this play.

title: Linguistic Strategies of Addresses at the Signing of the Education Bill (Extended Essay)
text:
Education is important and necessary for everyone in any country. The United States has made an effort to provide equal education for every American and its presidents have made legislation to resolve various issues of education. The Elementary and Secondary Education Act (ESEA) was enacted in 1965, under President Lyndon B. Johnson. This law is a part of the ‘War on Poverty’ and aims to address poverty issues in education and create high-quality and equitable education. In 2002, President George W. Bush introduced The No Child Left Behind Act (NCLB) to improve academic achievement among children from low-income and minority backgrounds. According to the U.S. Department of Education, “President Bush emphasized his deep belief in our public schools, but an even greater concern that "too many of our neediest children are being left behind," despite the nearly $200 billion in Federal spending since the passage of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act of 1965 (ESEA).”. The goal was to reduce achievement gaps and provide equal educational opportunities for all children. In 2015, President Obama signed The Every Student Succeeds Act (ESSA), which aimed to provide high-quality education fairly to all children and reduce educational achievement gaps. ESSA was an improvement of the NCLB legislation.
During the final stage of the legislative process when the president signed the bill, the three presidents delivered speeches. This study aims to examine the persuasive strategies used in these three speeches. It will analyze linguistic elements such as anaphora, personal pronouns, hyperbole, metaphor, and strategies such as Ethos, Pathos, and Logos to compare and contrast the language used in these speeches. Although the detailed contents of the three acts are different, their purposes and goals are quite similar. By examining the speeches given by the three presidents regarding these closely aligned bills, we can observe similarities and differences in their persuasive strategies and linguistic elements used.
Anaphora is “the practice in literature or rhetoric (= speech or writing intended to impress or persuade people) of repeating the same word at the start of several sentences to achieve an effect”. There are repeating specific expressions in the three speeches. These repetitions serve to emphasize key points, make them memorable, and create an emotional impact.
In the excerpt from the ESEA speech, the pronoun “we” is repeated at the beginning of each of the four sentences.
In this passage, the speaker discusses the significance that can be obtained from the passage of the ESEA bill. By repeating the word “we” at the beginning of each sentence, the speaker emphasizes the content and delivers it with greater impact and persuasiveness. In particular, the word “we” helps to connect the speaker and the audience as one community or group, narrowing the psychological distance and enhancing the effectiveness and persuasiveness of the message.
In this passage, the phrase “As…” is repeated three times. It expresses the thoughts, empathy, and expectations that he could have as a son, a former teacher, and a President. Additionally, the use of similar sentence structures adds impact to the message. In the NCLB speech, “the effort” is repeated like this, “... the effort to defend freedom and to defend our people, the effort to rout out terror wherever it exists, is noble and just and right, and your great country will prevail in this effort.”
The repetition of the phrase “the effort” is used to convey to the audience that the nation is making these efforts. By repeating the word “effort,” the speaker emphasizes the contributions and endeavors of the nation.
In the ESSA speech, President Obama mentioned supporters of the legislation in the following manner.
The legislation is highlighted as an important bill supported by significant organizations such as “teachers unions”, “civil rights organizations”, and “philanthropies”. This emphasis is intended to instill trust in the audience by showing it is supported by these influential groups.
The pronouns have an impact on forming a relationship with the audience. Jessica Håkansson’s study defines “the pronoun I is used when the speaker wants to speak as an individual rather than as a representative of a group and the pronoun we is used to invoke a sense of collectivity and to share responsibility”.
The ESEA speech used the pronoun “I” most. This speech frequently includes passages where the President expresses his thoughts and emotions as such.
The President used these sentences and present the reasons and justifications for enacting the legislation and often speaks about his choices and responsibilities.
By using “we” as the subject, the President tries to establish a sense of unity and encourage the public to align with his vision and intentions.
In the NCLB and ESSA speeches, the pronoun “we” is used most frequently as the subject. The use of the pronoun “we” aims to create a closer psychological distance between the President and the audience, and encourage the audience to align with the President's actions for education. In sentences where “I” is used as the subject in the NCLB speech, such as “I long for peace,” the President expresses his aspirations and goals.
In sentences like this, using “we” expands the subject of solving the education issues facing the United States beyond just the President or the government and includes the audience. It emphasizes collective responsibility and collaboration in solving education problems. Phrases like “And we owe the children of America a good education” and “We believe every child can learn” aim to foster a sense of shared commitment and alignment between the President's goals for achieving educational equity and the audience's own aspirations.
The phrase “Today, I’m proud to sign a law that’s going to make sure that every student is prepared to succeed in the 21st century.” from the ESSA speech reflects the President's positive mindset and confidence in the legislation. It conveys the President's pride in signing the law and his belief that it will be effective.
Hyperbole is “a way of speaking or writing that makes someone or something sound much bigger, better, smaller, worse, more unusual, etc., than they are”. “It consists of exaggerating some part of your statement in order to give it emphasis or focus. Hyperbole is never meant to be understood literally by the reader, …”
There is some hyperbole in the ESEA speech. The first expression, “acrimonious political feelings excited,” is a phrase used to point out the delay in educational improvement due to political issues by quoting the statement of President Mirabeau B. Lamar. This phrase uses “acrimonious” to emphasize the negative impact.
The second expression is “a fierce commitment to the ideal of education” It reveals the President’s volition in the reform of education. In particular, the word “fierce” emphasizes it.
The third expression is “ … this legislation will be remembered in history as men and women who began a new day of greatness in American society.”. Through the use of “a new day of greatness”, it speaks to the enactment of this bill, as historical, significant, and exceptional.
The fourth expression, “As President of the United States, I believe deeply no law I have signed or will ever sign means more to the future of America.” is used to show that this bill is extremely important. In the NCLB speech, a total of four hyperbolic expressions were used. The first expression is “… the effort that this great country is engaged in, the effort to defend freedom and to defend our people, the effort to rout out terror wherever it exists, is noble and just and right, and your great country will prevail in this effort.”. It uses exaggeration to claim that the country is making a lot of effort. It also highlights the importance of the efforts by appreciating the value of them.
The second expression is “And today begins a new era, a new time in public education in our country. As of this hour, America's schools will be on a new path of reform, and a new path of results.”. This passage employs the expressions “a new era” and “a new path” to emphasize the transformative nature of the legislation. By using these phrases, the President exaggerates the potential impact of the bill, suggesting that it will bring about significant changes in education.
The third expression is “The story of children being just shuffled through the system is one of the saddest stories of America.”. By sharing the story of marginalized children in education, the President highlights the gravity of the problem. He describes it as “one of the saddest stories.” This emphasizes the significance of the issue.
The fourth expression is “Signing this bill is the end of a long, long time of people sitting in rooms trying to hammer out differences.”. Signing a bill is the last step in legislation and can be said to be the end of many efforts to make it. It dramatizes the difficulty of the legislative process and underscores the achievement of reaching a consensus.
In the ESSA speech, the use of hyperbole is relatively limited. There is a hyperbolic expression used. The expression is “There’s nothing more essential to living up to the ideals of this nation than making sure every child is able to achieve their God-given potential.”. This statement emphasizes the importance of unlocking children's potential, indicating that the legislation plays a crucial role in enabling children to reach their full potential.
A metaphor is “an expression that describes a person or object by referring to something that is considered to possess similar characteristics”. “a metaphor speaks of one thing as though it actually were another. … It can help your readers see something as you want them to see it-to convey not just the literal truths of a thing, but the emotional or psychological truths of it as well.” There are many metaphors in all three addresses.
There are six metaphorical expressions used in the ESEA speech. The first one is “magic time.” “Magic time” is a positive expression of the speaker's personal experience with education, creating a sense of wonder and mystery around education. It also showcases the speaker's ideal vision of education and demonstrates their determination for educational reform.
The second one is “a fierce commitment”. This expression also reveals the determination for educational reform. “A fierce commitment” metaphorically represents a strong determination to achieve the ideals of education.
The third one is “the guardian genius of democracy . . . the only dictator that free men acknowledge and the only security that free men desire.” This expression is a quotation from President Lamar, referring to education. This expression presents education as a sacred, great, and significant entity. Particularly, this metaphor is expected to effectively resonate with Americans living in a democratic system.
The fourth one is “a major new commitment of the Federal Government to quality and equality in the schooling that we offer our young people.” “A major new commitment” represents the ESEA legislation and its goals. By promising the improvement of education quality and equality, the government instills trust in the audience through this metaphor.
The fifth one is “the revolution of the spirit against the tyranny of ignorance.” This refers to the enhancement of educational achievement and the resolution of educational inequality, which is the essence of the ESEA legislation. Therefore, this expression reinforces the significance and magnitude of the legislation.
The sixth one is “I know that education is the only valid passport from poverty.” “Valid passport” symbolizes a means to escape poverty, and that means education. Thus, this statement highlights the importance of education.
There are four metaphorical expressions used in the NCLB speech. The first one is “the precious gift.” Freedom is expressed as a precious gift. This signifies the importance of freedom.
The second one is “the legacy”. This expression refers to the NCLB legislation and emphasizes that the legislation will be significant and long-lasting.
The third one is “the war against illiteracy.” It represents the issue of illiteracy as a social problem, not a physical war. By framing it as a war, it intensifies the expression and highlights the urgency of resolving this problem.
The fourth one is “noble cause.” This expression is used to encourage citizens, the audience, to participate in making sure no child is left behind. It aims to make their efforts sound positive and remarkable.
There are five metaphorical expressions used in the ESSA speech. The first one is “an early Christmas present.” At the beginning of the speech, Obama introduced the ESSA legislation as a Christmas present. This aims to create a more favorable perception of the legislation and spark interest and curiosity among the audience.
The second one is “cookie-cutter reforms.” This is a negative expression used to describe the NCLB legislation that Obama intends to change. The term “cookie-cutter” conveys the perception that the legislation is rigid and inflexible. This effectively emphasizes the need for ESSA legislation.
The third one is “a Race to the Top.” This expression portrays the government's goals as being in a highly elevated and noble position. By using the term “Race,” conveys the message that the government is vigorously striving and making efforts. It effectively highlights the government's commitment.
The fourth one is “God-given potential”. This expression refers to the talents of children and portrays them as something sacred and divine, emphasizing their greatness and importance. It also supports the significance of education.
VI. Ethos “Ethos is frequently translated as some variation of “credibility or trustworthiness,” but it originally referred to the elements of a speech that reflected on the particular character of the speaker or the speech’s author.”
These passages appeal to audiences by showing the efforts of the people who made the bill and the personal status of the president himself.
In this passage, the President mentions his humble background to emphasize the importance of education and showcase his credibility. It implies to the audience that the President genuinely understands the value of education.
These sentences appeal ethically by referring to the various efforts of the government and the efforts of those who contributed to the creation of the bill.
In this way, the president is making an ethical appeal by referring to the government's efforts, efforts to make a bill, or by referring to supporters of the bill.
VII. Pathos “Pathos is frequently translated as some variation of “emotional appeal,” but it originally referred to the elements of a speech that appealed to any of an audience’s sensibilities.” It is a appealing to an audience’s emotion.
In this passage, the President shares their personal experiences related to education and introduces a person named Miss Katie Deadrich, aiming to touch the hearts of the audience.
In this passage, he talks about the value he pursues and the importance of it and appeals emotionally.
This passage urges the audience to take action together. By directly stating “it's up to you,” it delivers a strong and compelling message to the audience, calling on them to demand high standards and ensure that no child is left behind.
This passage describes the president's personal experience. They narrate witnessing students unleashing their potential and positively convey their involvement in that experience, emotionally connecting with the audience.
VIII. Logos “Logos is frequently translated as some variation of “logic or reasoning,” but it originally referred to the actual content of a speech and how it was organized.” It is a persuasion with strong logic and reason.
It explains the problems that education has experienced so far and explains why education reform is needed and why legislation should be enacted.
These are all introductions to the Bill and explain how to achieve educational goals. Therefore, these phrases explain the need for this Bill.
The three speeches all include anaphora, personal pronouns, hyperbole, metaphor, Ethos, Pathos, and Logos, and each of these linguistic elements effectively contributes to the speeches.
In the three speeches, anaphora is used by repetitively employing similar expressions. This technique emphasizes the importance of the legislation, the nation's efforts, etc., and aims to leave a lasting impression on the audience, reinforcing the significance of the legislation and building trust from the audience towards the nation's efforts.
Personal pronouns, particularly the use of “I” by the presidents, serve to express their thoughts and emotions, as well as to demonstrate the reasons and determination behind the legislation. The use of “We” aims to narrow the psychological distance between the presidents and the audience, urging the audience to align with their intentions and take collective action to address the issues.
Hyperbole is utilized to accentuate the education issues negatively or emphasize the positive effects of the legislation, thereby highlighting the importance of the legislation more forcefully and distinctly. Additionally, it exaggerates the efforts made to formulate the legislation, creating a sense of grandeur and emphasizing the magnitude of those efforts.
The metaphor effectively reveals the presidents' determination for education reform and effectively communicates the importance of education or education reform, including the significance of the legislation.
Ethos is commonly included in the ESEA, NCLB, and ESSA speeches. It is mainly used to mention the individuals or government officials who made efforts to create the legislation and to inform the audience about their dedication and sacrifices. This enhances the credibility of the speakers and the trustworthiness of their speeches. Pathos appeals to the audience's emotions by sharing the personal experiences or emotions of the presidents, evoking empathy and fostering positive perceptions of the role of education or addressing education issues. Furthermore, Logos is employed to explain the reasons for the need for education legislation and justify the enactment of the legislation.
The speeches share a common theme of portraying education as noble and significant, strongly emphasizing the need for education reform. This effectively justifies the formulation of the legislation and persuades the public. The linguistic techniques and persuasive strategies employed in the speeches contribute to their effectiveness. These speeches likely aided the presidents in enacting education legislation and implementing various reforms.

title: Director's Notebook: Hamlet
text:
I thought that there is a similarity between Hamlet and Laertes in the sense that both characters look for revenge after losing their fathers. I came up with the idea of focusing on Laertes as the main character and showing off to audiences his revenge process on stage. While the original play centers around Hamlet and draws attention to his revenge process, in my play, I decided to shift the focus to Laertes and highlight his revenge process. To show Laertes' revenge process, I selected four scenes from the play where Laertes appears, and I connected these scenes to create a play that focuses on showing audiences Laertes' revenge process.
a. Scene 1 The first scene shows when Laertes, after losing his father Polonius, goes to the king to listen to answers about his father's death. In this scene, Laertes is angry and stands up to the king, expressing his anger and demanding to know where his father is. The king insists on his innocence. Shortly after, Laertes' sister Ophelia appears. She is mad and insane from the shock of their father's death. Watching Ophelia's insanity, Laertes becomes even more decided to revenge for his father's enemy.
b. Scene 2 The king and Laertes meet and discuss their plan for revenge against Hamlet. They arrange a duel(single combat) between Hamlet and Laertes, intending to make them fight with poisoned swords. They also prepare a cup of alcoholic drink that is poisoned as a backup plan in case the sword does not kill Hamlet. While plotting Hamlet's death, Laertes receives news from the queen that Ophelia has died.
c. Scene 3 Laertes, the king, and the queen gather for Ophelia's funeral. Hamlet comes there and interrupts the funeral. He becomes very angry and fights with Laertes. Laertes remains unstoppable in his pursuit of revenge, waiting for the day of revenge against Hamlet. d. Scene 4 The day of the duel arrives, and Laertes and Hamlet meet with their swords. They start a duel, but an unexpected turn of events happens when the poisoned cup prepared by the king is drunk by the queen instead of Hamlet. The duel continues, and Hamlet is wounded by Laertes' poisoned sword. As the duel continued, the swords are swapped. Laertes is also wounded by the poisoned sword. The situation worsens, with the queen, Hamlet, and Laertes all giving in to the effects of the poison. Laertes confesses the truth to Hamlet, showing the king and himself as the guilty people. Hamlet uses the poisoned sword to kill the king. In the end, the king, queen, Laertes, and Hamlet all meet their death.
The 4 scenes that contain Laertes' revenge show things that are almost the same or different compared to Hamlet's revenge. While Hamlet is in internal conflict, Laertes' inner confusion is filled with a more and more strong desire for revenge. His thirst for revenge grows stronger, increasing the tension of the overall story. I aimed to make sure that the atmosphere and emotional strength flow without any breaks when connecting these 4 scenes together. Also, I wanted to clearly represent the changes in Laertes' emotions as they go through the process.
I acted Ophelia and Hamlet in the performance.
In Scene 1, Ophelia appears in a madness, insanity by the loss of her father, and She starts to talk to herself. I believed these lines show the shock and anger resulting from her father's death. To show Ophelia's disturbed mind, I constantly looked into empty space and shifted my look. Also, I varied my vocal tone to reveal her wild emotional ups and downs, changing outbursts to composed tones.
In Scene 3, Hamlet angrily faces Laertes, and when Laertes grabs Hamlet by the collar, he responds emotionally. However, as Hamlet is in a position of nobility, I wanted to avoid showing him in an informal manner. Therefore, in Scene 3, I raised my voice with anger but maintained a firm and controlled delivery, while keeping my actions. In almost the same way, in Scene 4, I aimed to show off Hamlet's behavior through exact movements and a composed firm vocal tone.
To prevent any confusion between Ophelia and Hamlet for the audience, Ophelia(I) wore a dress, while Hamlet(I) wore a shirt during the performance.
a. Monologue I take attention to "making Laertes the main character" in the direction, I focused on the monologue scene. In my opinion, monologues in a play often provide a deeper understanding of the inner thoughts of the main character. Also, the main characters involve the most interaction with other characters.
To make Laertes the main character, I decided to include added more monologue scenes that would allow the audience to see into Laertes' inner world. Through this, I aimed to show Laertes' emotions and the process of his emotional change.
b. Distant between characters Laertes reveals hostility to the king in scene 1. It is because Laertes is doubtful of the king and he has not yet had revenge against Hamlet. However, with the appearance of Ophelia, he decides revenge on his father and promises cooperation with the king. This change in Laertes's inner self was expressed through the physical distance between the characters. This is the position when Laertes first appeared.
Afterward, Ophelia appears, and because of her, Laertes's position changes. After Ophelia's exit, Laertes is closer to the king.
c. Costume and props Each character is distinguished by props or costumes. The king and queen wore different crowns.
Ophelia wore a dress.
Hamlet wore a shirt.
Laertes has no other props or costumes, but it is distinguishable because he is the only one who does not use costumes or props.
Ophelia brings out two flowers in scene one. They are rosemary and tricolored violets. The flower language of these flowers is "think of me" and "beautiful memories". Ophelia throws the flowers in front of Laertes as she exits. And Laertes picks up the flower and decides to take revenge on his father. Later, at Ophelia's funeral (Scene 3), Laertes appears with Ophelia's flowers and places them on her coffin. He remembers her through flowers and reveals his willingness to succeed in revenge.
In the duel scene between Hamlet and Laertes (Scene 4), they each appear with a sword. The sword plays an important role in the ending of the play. The appearance of the sword shows that their duel begins and also shows the beginning of the tragedy. The sword plays a role in leading them to death and becomes a tool for revenge.
Scene 3 Ophelia's coffin was planned to appear at Ophelia's funeral. We planned to make a square box-shaped coffin with form board, but we couldn't make it due to a lack of materials. Instead, it was expressed as a movement of walking with an invisible coffin to show the king and Laertes carrying a coffin together. Assuming that there was a coffin, they pretended to be holding something and kept the same speed to walk in balance.
In the play, the king and queen are often sitting on chairs. This shows the authority of the king and queen. I wanted to raise the physical height, but this was impossible because the stage was narrow and the props we had were limited. The king and queen sit in chairs, meet those who come to them, and watch the duel scene.
d. Light The play consists of a total of four scenes, and during scene changes, we used to turn the lights off and on to show the change. In the scene where they start a duel with their swords, we presented the actions as if showing a series of photographs. We over and over again turned the lights off and on for each action.
The sequence of actions included: The movement of fighting with swords, The movement of striking each other's swords, causing them to drop, The movement of picking up the fallen swords, The movement of Laertes causing a wound on Hamlet with his sword, The movement of Hamlet stabbing Laertes in the stomach with his sword, The final movement of the Queen falling.
By presenting the tragedy through these actions, we aimed to show it goes strength and make tension. We faced the challenge of how to show this duel scene, as we are not professional actors. I thought focusing on the sound of sword fighting while keeping the lights off wouldn't be good enough to improve the atmosphere. Therefore, we chose to present the actions in a frozen state. This decision was the result of much serious thought and working in a group to get ideas. Also, we received helpful input from 태민's thinking about the lighting used in this scene.
For Ophelia's funeral, I used pale blue lighting to express Laertes' sadness. To show death, I used red lighting. This was done to create a visual effect of the characters facing their death. The red lighting was starting with the Queen's death and continued as Hamlet and Laertes suffered their wounds and met their unavoidable death. As Hamlet killed the King and then himself and Laertes also met his end, deaths overall gave to the sad atmosphere. Therefore, we used red lighting to make it with the mood of the play.
Pin lighting was used to show the monologue scene.
e. Music Five pieces of music were used in the play. These have different atmospheres from each other and they make the tension of the play. The first music was calm and dark and it was used in the scene of the queen informing Ophelia's death to Laertes. The second music is calm and sad music, and it was used at Ophelia's funeral. The third music is music that slowly changes from a calm and dark atmosphere to a dynamic and dark atmosphere, and it was used since the queen drank poison. The fourth music is passionate and dark, and it was used since the duel between Hamlet and Laertes began again. From here, a tragic atmosphere is formed. The last piece of music was heavy and dark and it was used in the scene of Laertes's monologue when he was left alone after Hamlet and the king's death. The music continued until Laertes fell down and died after finishing his lines. It could give the audience a lingering impression.
The five pieces of music contributed to the development of the atmosphere and the formation of the tragic atmosphere.
The sound effects of the knife hitting and the fanfare were also used. These sound effects were used to inform the audience by the sound that the duel would begin or that the duel is going on.
After setting the scene and writing the script, we went through the process of organizing and modifying the movement. The movement line was modified in consideration of changes in the position of lights and characters. Next, a script reading was conducted. Then, the lights used in the duel scene were specifically planned.
After this, the actors' movements were practiced. 성혁, who plays the queen, practiced playing the scene of falling down after drinking poison. After that, we practiced the whole scene.
During the exercise, we discussed the flow of emotions for each character. The atmosphere of the play rises as a whole and flows toward a tragic end. In consideration of this, we thought about what emotional changes the characters would experience. And we also thought about what kind of voice the character should make in each scene and what gestures to make.
Then, during the rehearsal, we could get feedback from my teacher and friends. The biggest problem in our performance was that audiences couldn't hear the voices of the characters well. The music had to be turned down and the characters' voices had to be louder. And until this time, it had not decided on the costumes of Hamlet and Ophelia, but costumes were needed to distinguish the two characters. We also had to make a bigger move to increase the dynamic in the duel scene. And it was necessary to make Hamlet's movements more neat. We were able to make a better play in the final performance by reflecting on this feedback.
Actually, there were conflicts in the practice process. One of the team members did not continue to participate in the practice, causing problems in the practice process. However, we encouraged the team members or gave them advice and warnings so that everyone could participate in the practice as much as possible. Through the efforts of the team members, we were able to practice several times and complete the final performance.
I played a lot of roles in making my play, such as choosing the scenes, writing scripts, planning movements and lighting, editing sound and pieces of music, and setting and making props. As a director, I organized the stage visually and auditory and prepared the necessary things like music and props. I edited the music to be used in the play and made Ophelia's flowers, which we did not buy as a prop.
In addition, in practice, as a director, I directed actors to move and act according to the intention of directing. And, I discussed the emotions and behaviors of the characters with the actors.
And I played Hamlet and Ophelia as actors in the performance. I had to play two characters, Hamlet and Ophelia, so I needed to play the characteristics of the two characters accurately. I thought about how to play these two characters differently and applied them directly to the acting.(as described in "3. Characters")
It's disappointing that some of the lines were not effectively brought across during our performance. As Shakespeare's works are unique in their lines and language, the lines in this play were extremely important. Also, it was unfortunate to my voice didn't deliver well to the audience.
During the directing process, I felt that the play's atmosphere was dull and flat before adding some music. To solve this, I added music, and I realized the significant effect it had on shaping the mood of the play. Music had the power to create the atmosphere depending on it.
Also, the process of thinking about how to make Laertes the main character led me to dig deeply into the character's role. I thought carefully about how to express the main character's inner world and the level of interaction with other characters. Through this, I gained a better understanding of the presence of the main character in the play.
As an actor, I played both Ophelia and Hamlet. Playing two characters in a single performance was not an easy job. I had to make sure that the audience could clearly tell the difference between the characters I showed, and I needed to put myself in the fitting emotions for each character. This led me to think about and think about the particular emotions and actions of each character in a more describe. It gave me an understanding of what actors should think about and think about/believe when showing a character, and this exploration of things deeply gave to my understanding of Hamlet and Ophelia.

title: English Theater Journal (reflections)
text:
Today, I learned about using the subjunctive mood with "if" from my teacher. We practiced answering questions while creating hypothetical statements using the format of the if-clause. It was challenging to speak the sentences immediately and naturally. However, after practicing by speaking out loud a few times, I quickly adapted to the format of the if-clause and became faster at creating sentences.
I discovered that practicing sentence structures repeatedly and speaking them out loud helps with speaking more naturally. If I apply this concept to acting, I think that reading lines out loud is much more effective for memorizing dialogue than simply reading them silently. Also I think speaking the lines aloud can aid in delivering them more smoothly and clearly. Does "speaking" really make theater practice effective?
I watched a theater video "The Caucasian Chalk Circle". The protagonist, Grusha, discovers and raises the governor's child, and she sets off on her journey. This play explores motherly love and justice. It poses some questions to the audience: Who is a ‘true’ mother? What defines ‘justice’?
One characteristic of "The Caucasian Chalk Circle", is the use of a flexible stage. The stage setting changes as needed when transitioning between scenes, and sometimes the stage is changed while the characters are in motion. Another unique characteristic is the live music performance. It was the first time I saw a theatrical production with live music. While I watched the performance in a video, I imagine that those who experienced it in person felt a richer auditory experience.
The third characteristic is the involvement of the audience on the stage. As the stage transformed its shape, the audience had to move together. It creates a sense of immersion within the performance.
As a director and theater student, I was amazed to discover that stage directing could be done in such a way, and it was an opportunity to learn new stage-directing techniques. The idea of transforming the stage on the spot was something I had never imagined. It seemed incredibly challenging. I wonder how this flexible stage was born and how much it is used in the present.
I prepared for a presentation with my teammate Our team decided to present on Kathakali, so we began our research on Kathakali. We first determined how to structure our presentation. We looked into the origins, history, themes of the performance, costumes, makeup, movements, dance, and music of Kathakali.
One of the most impressive features of Kathakali is the dance using hand gestures. Each specific hand gesture carries its own meaning, and there are various hand gestures. It attracted me how these hand gestures are combined to create a dance. I realized that every small detail adds depth to the performance. It made me decide to be a director who incorporates meaning into each detail.
Furthermore, Kathakali creates a special performance without elaborate stage devices. The costumes, makeup, music, and dance come together to produce a rich and captivating performance. These elements may seem basic in theater, but they are all unique to Kathakali. I thought that this aspect made Kathakali a distinctive form of performance. When in class, I didn't search for what meaning the Kathakali costume has, but I want to know about it.
In plays where multiple characters appear, usually, different actors act on each character. However, in Rakugo, one person expressed multiple characters by changing their gaze, speech, and voice. Various characters are not represented through makeup or costumes, but gazes and speech instead.
In the Chinese Shadow Play, I noticed that the puppets had an incredible number of joints, which made their movements flexible. The techniques used to manipulate the puppets created dynamic movements, which was fascinating. Conducting a Shadow Play requires meticulous and skilled techniques. Moreover, there were quite a few characters and background elements involved in the Shadow Play. I didn't know much about Shadow Plays before, but it was impressive to see how such a seemingly simple tool could create a rich and captivating performance.
I wanted to learn more about multiple roles because it was so interesting that Rakugoka act multiple roles.
Today was our group's turn to make a presentation and we presented the contents of the Kathakali we prepared. I had to demonstrate Katakali's movements in the presentation myself. I tried my best to demonstrate as I practiced, but it wasn't satisfying that I didn't think the true atmosphere of Katakali was revealed well. I knew through research that Katakali was a difficult dance that required high skill and a lot of practice, and I could see the reason by practicing and demonstrating it myself. I found that all physical elements, not only hands, and feet, but also facial expressions and gaze, should be cared for, and these detailed elements were very important points in the play. After the presentation, we listened to the feedback on the presentation with our friends and teacher and talked about Kathakali. As we talked, we came to talk about why old plays such as Katakali show a strong religious character. We thought that people used to think of God as important, but as time went by, people became more important to humans. So the old one was more about God and religion, and the recent one was more about humans. And I wonder if this will actually be the case.
I discovered that Kabuki, known for its unique makeup, also focuses on various stage settings, which was quite new to me. It's interesting to learn that Kabuki has utilized complex and elaborate stage designs, including Hinamichi, Seri, and revolving stages from ancient times. Additionally, both Rakugo and Kabuki are traditional Japanese theater forms. However, while Rakugo uses a simple stage, Kabuki uses an intricate stage. It's amazing to see how different forms of theater have emerged and continued within the same country. Kabuki also has a similarity with Kathakali. They express their character through the color of their makeup. It is a play that was born within other cultures, but it has something in common.
I'm curious about the Renaissance theater, where performances took place outdoors without the use of lighting and curtains. I wonder what kind of agreement or understanding existed between the actors and the audience in such settings. Other traditional theater forms often rely heavily on visual elements like dance, and music for expression. In contrast, it's interesting that Renaissance theater relies on dialogue. With an emphasis on dialogue, the plot must be important in this form of theater.
I'm curious to know if there is always only one dalang in every performance and who plays the musical instruments and how many musicians are involved. I'm also interested in learning about the main themes and stories depicted in the performances. It's interesting to see how art and culture come together through such diverse elements in puppetry and shadow play.
Wayang Kulit seemed to have similarities because it was a play born in India like Kathakali. I looked for it because I wondered if the two plays had anything in common.
Today, teacher told us the “blocking” and work order. And our team decided on the scene to perform. I thought about which scene to perform. I was interested in the relationship between Hamlet and Laertes, so I compared the characteristics of these two. The two characters certainly had different personalities, but the situation and tragedies they faced were similar. I wanted to show the similarity between Hamlet and Laertes in my performance. In the original work, the situation develops with a focus on Hamlet. I wanted to focus on Laertes and show the situation goes. How to focus on Laertes seemed to be the key to the performance. I was very worried about this part. How to make Laertes the main character? In order to answer the question, I had to first answer the question of how to make a specific character the main character in the play. The exact answer to this question has not yet been made. So, I extracted and organized all the scenes in the original film in which Laertes appears.
First, I thought about how to highlight Laertes as the main character. As the main character, I thought about different ways to bring attention to the character and decided that it would be clear to show/tell about the character's internal to the audience. I thought it was important to show Laertes's inner confusion for the audience's understanding emotion of Laertes. Also, I came up with the "blocking" that I learned in the last lesson. I decided to place Laertes in the center to focus more on him.
Secondly, I thought about how to slowly raise the atmosphere of the play. I thought of two ways: to use music and to slowly increase actors' feelings in a performance. This approach can effectively add to creating tension and increasing the overall atmosphere of the play. Thirdly, I was wondering how to smoothly switch between scenes that were disconnected from each other. To solve this problem, I decided to use lighting. Laertes appears as a supporting character in the original work, so his scenes are often short and disconnected. For smooth flow, I will add Laertes's monologue and use the light signal to switch from one scene to another visually smoothly.
Today was the day to perform we had prepared so far. Three groups performed in the order of "The Laramie Project", "Hamlet", and "A Midsummer Night's Dream". Among them, the performance of "The Laramie Project" was very impressive. This is because the form of the play was very new and unique. They cut the interview scene short and showed it, but only the interview scene delivered the entire story to the audience. Nor did they limit their stage to just "the stage". I was very surprised at this part. As a director of another work, I think I had a really meaningful experience. I felt like I saw a completely new play than I had ever seen. I think this experience will help me to create more diverse and creative productions in the future.
I became interested in the unique theatrical form of "The Laramie Project" and wanted to find more information about this work.
